title: Agentic Postgres generated outputs
description: The automation contract, version 5. One versioned schema, two document kinds, discriminated by a required `document_kind` const and separated by a oneOf so a rendered document can never validate as deployed state. `rendered` is a pure function of the digested inputs and contains no timestamp, no observed value and no provider identifier. `deployed` is a published observation of a converged host and contains all three. additionalProperties is false at every level of both branches. Version 3 added the Session 3 database block -- container identity, memory budget, and observed cluster facts -- and split the formerly shared `database` definition in two so that `observed` is unrepresentable on the rendered branch. Version 4 added `database.access_profiles`, three ways to reach the two transports (ADR 0041), and closed the endpoint conditional so that an `available` endpoint must actually carry a host, a port, a password-free URL and a secret reference. Version 5 is entirely on the deployed branch (ADR 0053): `routes` gains `rest` and `docs` as status-carrying objects beside `health`, a new `api` block records what the published surface actually serves, `jwt` appears for the first time carrying public metadata only, and `database.observed` gains the `instance_uuid` the port registry is keyed by. Version 12 is Session 8's, and it is entirely on the deployed branch: `routes.mcp` -- named by the rendered branch since version 1 and never published here (D395) -- and an `mcp` block carrying the protocol revision, the authorization profile's honest non-conformance, the accepted token use (ADR 0115) and the capability lock's identity. Chosen ONCE from the session's whole surface rather than a run at a time, because D255 and D308 are the record of the alternative. See docs/decisions/0012-output-document-kinds.md, docs/decisions/0027-the-output-schema-gains-a-version-and-a-migration-path.md, docs/decisions/0041-two-transports-three-access-profiles.md, docs/decisions/0051-the-bootstrap-issuer-is-temporary-and-carries-its-own-expiry.md, docs/decisions/0053-outputs-version-5.md and docs/decisions/0115-the-agent-plane-accepts-only-agent-tokens.md. Version 13 is Session 10's, and it is the only version to touch both branches at once: `backup` becomes a shared definition carrying the repository's bucket and `retain_full` -- a bound the schema had declared and no code had ever read (D519) -- the rendered branch's `compose.networks` gains the egress network the cluster reaches its repository over (D516), and the deployed branch gains `backup_state`, the first place this document can say when a backup last succeeded and whether WAL is reaching the repository. `backup_state` is separate from `backup` rather than nested inside it so that an observation stays unrepresentable on the rendered branch (ADR 0012) WITHOUT duplicating the settings into two defs, which is the copy D389 warns about. See docs/decisions/0146-outputs-version-13.md.

inputs.description: Every file that determines this render. The same block appears in each generated file, so an incomplete set is detectable. secrets_contract_sha256 joined the set in Session 2 when secrets.required_names started reaching rendered output: a value derived from a file that is not digested here would make the render depend on an untracked input.

generated_directory.description: Repository-relative, and deliberately still so in v2. Host paths live on the deployed branch under `runtime`, with their own anchored absolute patterns; loosening this one to carry both meanings is how a path-traversal check dies.

networks.description: Version 13 added `backup`: an egress network of the cluster's own, because `internal` is `internal: true` and has no route off the host (measured, D516), so `archive-push` cannot reach R2 from where the postmaster runs it. `edge` would work and is refused -- it is where Traefik's public side lives. Named here a run before anything attaches to it; the rendered branch names what a deployment WOULD create, and `storage.bucket` sat in exactly this state from Session 1 to Session 7.

health.description: An object rather than a bare URL so the rendered and deployed branches stay structurally parallel: the deployed document has to carry a readiness claim, and a claim needs somewhere to live.

metrics.description: Version 14. The metrics surface ADR 0005 reserved in Session 1 and nothing owned for thirteen sessions (D760) -- a reserved path is a promise the platform makes about a route it will one day own, and a route the deployed document does not name is a promise nothing can find. A bare URL here and a publishedRoute on the deployed branch, like every route added since version 5: the render describes what would be created, and the readiness claim belongs where something can observe it. `health` is the exception rather than the model, and predates publishedRoute.

storage.description: Version 11. The object-storage surface's URL, derived by `naming` like every other route here and published whether or not storage is enabled -- a rendered document names what a deployment would create, and the readiness claim lives on the deployed branch.

secrets.description: Names only. No value, no reference to a materialized path, no generation identifier -- a rendered document describes a plan, and nothing has been materialized when it is written.

deployedDocument.description: Root-owned, mode 0600, written under /etc/agentic-postgres/projects/{project_key}/ only after successful convergence. It is a published observation, not the authority for provider ownership -- that is bootstrap-state.json. It carries provider IDs and client IDs; it never carries a client secret, an access token, a sentinel value, a secret checksum or a credential-bearing URL.

deployed_through_session.description: The session this project was deployed through. Read back by the systemd launcher at boot to choose the secret set and the Compose profiles, so that a restart brings up what the deploy brought up rather than a subset of it. Absent from the rendered branch by construction: a render deploys nothing. Minimum 2 because sessions before that start no container at all.

routes.description: Version 5 added `rest` and `docs` beside `health`, which Session 2 built as a status-carrying object for exactly this (ADR 0053). The rendered branch names the same three URLs and remains their single derivation; this branch records what is being served against them. Version 11 added `storage`. Version 12 added `mcp` -- which the RENDERED branch has named since version 1 and this one had never carried (D395). That is D389's shape exactly, in a second place: a route published in the document a manifest produces and absent from the document every plane reads. It is caught here before a host trip rather than by one. The two branches' route sets are compared AS SETS by a contract test, so the next route added to one and forgotten in the other fails offline.

health.description: The URL is present whatever the status, and deliberately so: the platform health path is the same string for every project whether or not it answers, and a null there would delete the address an operator needs in order to go and look. `rest` and `docs` are the other case -- see `publishedRoute`.

app.description: Version 9. The application API route, whose status is how a project says it is awaiting its first administrator (D230): `unavailable` with a null URL until one exists, exactly as `rest` was for a project deployed through session 4. A deployment state was considered and refused -- `publishedRoute` already expresses this and every reader already understands it.

app_docs.description: Version 9. The application API's documentation page: a second surface of the same documentation service (D226, ADR 0069), not a second service. `unavailable` until the surface is published.

storage.description: Version 11. The object-storage surface, and it follows `app` exactly (D326, D230's two-stage convergence): `unavailable` with a null URL until the R2 credential validates, the operator command printed, the deploy exiting 0, and `ready` on the redeploy that observes it. A dedicated `storage_credentials_required` deployment state was considered and refused for `app`'s reason -- `publishedRoute` already expresses this and every reader already understands it, while a second convergence mechanism would need its own tests, its own operator documentation and its own failure modes beside one that is deployed and proved on two projects.

metrics.description: Version 14, and it follows `mcp` exactly (D326 two-stage convergence): `unavailable` with a null URL until the collector answers on the route, `ready` on the deploy that observes it. The collector runs only for a deployment through session 14, so a project deployed through 13 names the route and reports it unavailable -- which is the honest pair, and the reason this is a status rather than an absence.

mcp.description: Version 12, and it follows `app` and `storage` exactly (D326's two-stage convergence): `unavailable` with a null URL until the agent plane is deployed and something answers on the route, `ready` on the deploy that observes it. The rendered branch has named this URL since version 1 and nothing has ever published its readiness -- D395. What the status is NOT is a claim about the MCP runtime's own protocol: that lives in `mcp`, beside `api`, and the two are bound by the same coherence rule `api` and `routes.rest` are (`_refuse_incoherent_publication`).

certificate_sha256.description: A fingerprint of a public certificate. Public material, so recording it leaks nothing; it is what lets the external suite prove it reached the same certificate the host issued.

fresh.description: False records a bounded last-known-good start. Recorded rather than hidden: a host that has been running on a stale generation is a fact an operator needs.

runtime.description: Absolute host paths, anchored. This is where Session 2's filesystem layout is represented, so project.generated_directory never has to stop being repository-relative.

renderedDatabase.description: Version 7. The rendered branch carries no `observed` block at all -- not an empty one, not a nulled one. ADR 0012 says a rendered document contains no observed value, and the cheapest way to keep that true is for the field to be unrepresentable here rather than merely constrained. That is why the two branches have separate definitions instead of one shared one. Version 4 added `access_profiles` (ADR 0041). Version 7 added `statement_timeouts` (ADR 0067). Version 8 added `api_connection_budget` (ADR 0070). Version 11 added `storage_connection_budget` and `pooler_pool_size` (ADR 0099).

auth_connection_budget.description: Version 10. How many cluster connections the auth service commits to: its pool plus its reservations. Published whether or not the service is enabled, so the bootstrap plane's division of the budget does not move when somebody toggles a flag. The third claimant on one `max_connections` (ADR 0070) -- and the reason that division is a function rather than a subtraction.

deployedDatabase.description: Version 7. Identical to the rendered branch plus `observed`, which is the only block here that is a measurement rather than a derivation. Version 8 added `api_connection_budget` (ADR 0070). Version 11 added `storage_connection_budget` and `pooler_pool_size` (ADR 0099).

auth_connection_budget.description: Version 10. How many cluster connections the auth service commits to: its pool plus its reservations. Published whether or not the service is enabled, so the bootstrap plane's division of the budget does not move when somebody toggles a flag. The third claimant on one `max_connections` (ADR 0070) -- and the reason that division is a function rather than a subtraction.

httpsOrigin.description: Scheme, host, optional port, and nothing else. Refuses a path, a query, a fragment, a wildcard, a userinfo component, plain http, and the literal `null` that a sandboxed iframe and a file:// document send -- an allowlist containing `null` admits anything that can arrange to be opaque. The same pattern `project.schema.json` uses for both origin lists, and it is written twice because the two schemas share no $defs; `test_the_origin_patterns_agree` is what keeps them one grammar.

storageConnectionBudget.description: Version 11. How many cluster connections the storage service commits to: its pool plus its reservations. The fourth claimant on one `max_connections` (ADR 0099), published whether or not storage is enabled for the reason the other three are -- the bootstrap plane's division must not move when somebody toggles a flag it does not read.

poolerPoolSize.description: Version 11. The pooler's server-side pool, `database.pool_size` from the manifest, published for exactly one purpose: so the bootstrap plane can check that what is LEFT for the application covers it (D327, ADR 0099). Two arithmetics exist over this budget -- the manifest charges this figure for the application, the bootstrap grants the application the remainder -- and nothing compared them until Session 7. They agreed by coincidence, 23 against 20. `default_pool_size` is per (user, database) and the application role is the pooler's only application user, so a remainder below this is a pool the pooler cannot fill, and PostgreSQL reports it as `too many connections for role` -- naming the role rather than the number.

statementTimeouts.description: Per-role `statement_timeout`, keyed by the **derived role name** rather than by the manifest's role suffix. The manifest keys `api.rest.statement_timeouts` by suffix; rendering resolves each suffix through `database.roles` and writes the result here, so the bootstrap plane applies a name it was given instead of deriving one (ADR 0002). A role named here that is absent from `database.roles` is unrepresentable by construction, because the only writer resolves through that map. Version 7, ADR 0067: before it, the manifest's timeouts were validated and then dropped at this boundary, so no request role ever received one.

^[a-z_][a-z0-9_]*$.description: A strict duration, the same grammar the manifest uses: digits and a unit, no space, no compound, no zero. PostgreSQL reads a bare integer as milliseconds and `0` as *disabled*, so a grammar admitting either would let a document turn a timeout off while looking like it set one.

api_documentation.description: Version 6. The role the OpenAPI capture and the documentation page read the published surface as. It holds view SELECT and EXECUTE on the write RPCs -- which is what makes `openapi-mode = follow-privileges` publish the whole surface -- and the pre-request hook refuses to establish an identity for it, so the RPCs it advertises are ones it can never perform. NOLOGIN: it is reached by SET ROLE from the authenticator, like anon and authenticated, and holds no credential of its own.

databaseBudget.description: Derived from the manifest, so it belongs on the rendered branch. `unreclaimable_mb` is the only computed member: it is what the host must actually find, because on a box with no swap page cache is reclaimable and shared memory is not. It is deliberately NOT equal to memory_limit_mb -- see the Session 3 plan 3.3 for the measurement that separated them.

databaseObserved.description: Measured against a running cluster, never derived. `not_observed` with five nulls is the honest state for a deployment that has not yet been read -- the same discipline `endpoint` uses, for the same reason: a zero or an empty object would be indistinguishable from a real measurement that happened to be empty. Version 5 added `instance_uuid`, which is a measurement in the strictest sense available here: it is a property of the data rather than of the configuration that produced it, and it is read out of the cluster by the same query the port allocator uses (ADR 0053, D106).

instance_uuid.description: `app_private.project_identity.instance_uuid`. The port-allocation registry is keyed by it and records the project key only for humans; until version 5 the deployed document carried no copy, so the access broker searched live allocations by key and refused ambiguity rather than resolving it. Present here so the broker can match on the identity the registry actually uses.

extensions.description: Installed extension name to installed version, read from pg_extension. Not pg_available_extensions: what is available is not what is installed, and the distinction is the whole content of DBX-PG-001.

oneOf.description: The three kept separate on purpose. A single `memory_mb` would average a reclaimable number together with an unreclaimable one and report something that is true of neither.

publishedRoute.description: A route this session publishes, and the honest way to say it was not published. `unavailable` forces a null URL -- unlike `health`, whose address exists for every project at every session. A deployment through session 4 serves no REST and no documentation, and naming a URL for a surface nothing is listening on would be exactly the failure `endpoint` was tightened in version 4 to prevent: a record that claims to exist and points at nothing.

deployedApi.description: What the published REST surface actually serves, version 5 (ADR 0053). Three checksums rather than one: the reviewed surface contract, the project-neutral canonical snapshot, and the per-project document actually published. A single 'contract checksum' would be unable to say which of the three moved, and the three move for different reasons -- a reviewed change, a PostgREST upgrade, and a project's own host and title. No direct service address appears: `postgrest:3000` is a runtime detail and a published one is a way around the edge's limits. No admin URL appears, because the admin surface binds container loopback and is not a network service.

status.description: `unavailable` is the state of every project deployed through a session before 5, and of a session-5 project whose REST surface did not come up. It forces every other member null, so a partially-filled block cannot be published as an observation.

exposed_schema.description: The one schema PostgREST is configured to expose. Recorded because `db-schemas` is the boundary that decides what a request can name at all, and a reader should not have to open a rendered configuration file to learn it.

connection_budget_reserved.description: What this service takes out of the cluster's connection budget: the pool, plus the LISTEN/NOTIFY connection the schema cache needs, plus startup and recovery headroom. Recorded rather than recomputed by a reader, because the number a reader would recompute is the one nobody checked against `max_connections`.

canonical_openapi_sha256.description: contracts/postgrest-openapi.canonical.json -- the generated, project-neutral snapshot two projects share (ADR 0050).

project_openapi_sha256.description: The document this project actually publishes, carrying its own host and title. Distinct from the canonical checksum by construction, and recorded so that 'the snapshot matches' can be a comparison rather than an assertion.

deployedMcp.description: What the published agent plane actually serves, version 12. Deliberately `deployedApi`'s shape rather than a new one: a status that forces every other member null, checksums that name the two artefacts a reader would otherwise have to guess were the same one, and no direct service address -- the MCP runtime's container port is a runtime detail and a published one is a way around the edge. What is NOT here is a connection budget, and its absence is the record: the MCP runtime holds no database credential, so it takes no share of ADR 0099's division (D407). A considered zero is written down the same way a cost is, because otherwise the next reader cannot tell it from an oversight -- which is what D309 was. Nothing here is a bound the runtime enforces: rows, elapsed time and affected rows are per-capability fields of the capability lock, whose identity is `capability_lock_sha256`, and publishing a second copy of them here would be two authorities for one number.

status.description: `unavailable` is the state of every project deployed through a session before 8, and of a session-8 project whose agent plane did not come up. It forces every other member null, so a partially-filled block cannot be published as an observation.

protocol_revision.description: The highest MCP protocol revision the deployed runtime IMPLEMENTS, read from the framework's own constant and never from a document that hoped for one. It read `negotiated` until Session 8 Run 4 measured what that word buys: a server handed an `initialize` for an older revision answers with that older revision, so a negotiated value is a fact about the CLIENT and would move when the probe moved while the deployment did not (ADR 0123, D428). `DEFAULT_NEGOTIATED_VERSION` is the neighbouring trap -- what an unversioned caller receives, two revisions below what this runtime speaks. The revision changes on a schedule nobody here controls, so it is an observation with a date shape rather than an enum this repository would have to chase. The pattern is a shape and not a claim about which revisions exist.

authorization_spec_conformant.description: Whether the agent plane's bearer profile conforms to the MCP authorization specification. It does not, and saying so is the point (D413): this deployment pre-provisions an internal bearer, and the honest record of that belongs in the document every plane reads rather than in prose in a runbook. A claim that lives only in prose is a claim nobody checks -- D274, where `/docs/rest` was proved at 401 and 200 for four runs and had never rendered.

accepted_token_use.description: The one `token_use` this surface accepts (ADR 0115), published as a field for D413's reason. The enum has one member and is not the union of `claims.TOKEN_USES`: `access` is what the APPLICATION API accepts (ADR 0114), and a schema that permitted either here would validate a deployment that had quietly changed its mind. The two surfaces are mirror images and a test asserts the two constants differ.

capability_contract_sha256.description: contracts/snapshots/mcp/mcp-capabilities.canonical.json -- the project-neutral compiled capability contract two projects share, in `api_surface_sha256`'s role.

capability_lock_sha256.description: The DEPLOYED lock, resolving this project's own paths -- the artefact the runtime obeys. Distinct from the canonical contract by construction, and recorded so that 'the runtime serves what was reviewed' can be a comparison rather than an assertion. A lock built from an unreviewed OpenAPI capture is a capability surface nobody approved, which is the failure `capabilities.yaml` exists to prevent.

tool_count.description: How many tools the deployed lock registers. Published rather than left to the lock's digest because a digest says two things differ and never says how: a lock that grew a fifth tool and a lock whose description was reworded are the same event to a checksum. The bound is not the count Session 8 expects -- that is a contract test's business -- it is the range beyond which a number is a bug rather than a surface.

deployedJwt.description: Public token metadata, version 5 (ADR 0051, ADR 0053). Every member here is something a verifier is entitled to hold: an issuer, an audience, an algorithm, key identifiers and a digest of the public JWKS. No private JWK, no signing key reference and no token appears -- not as a redacted field, not as a reference, not at all. `temporary` is state a later gate reads rather than prose nobody executes: SEC-BOOT-001 compares it against `deployed_through_session` and goes red on the deployment that should have replaced the bootstrap issuer.

issuer.description: The same string the rendered branch derives. It does not have to be dereferenceable in session 5; it has to be stable, because session 6 issues against it.

algorithm.description: Asymmetric, so the verifier holds no material that can sign. A symmetric algorithm would make every verifier an issuer, which is the property ADR 0051 refuses.

oneOf.description: The active key, and during a documented rotation overlap the one retiring key. Two is the ceiling on purpose: an unbounded set is a set nobody retires from.

retire_after.description: The deadline the temporary issuer carries with it. Null when no rotation is in flight; a date when one is, so that 'the overlap window' is a value rather than an intention.

oneOf.description: Consumer name to the sha256 of the public JWKS that consumer has actually loaded. Keyed by consumer because propagation is per consumer: a rotation that promoted on the strength of one verifier having reloaded would be promoting on an assumption about the others.

verifier_acknowledgements.description: Version 9. What makes promotion safe rather than hopeful (plan section 4): a prepared key is promoted only once every verifier has acknowledged the same digest. Recorded rather than inferred -- `public_jwks_sha256` says what the issuer published, and this says what was picked up, and the whole point is that the two can differ for a while.

sha256.description: Lowercase hexadecimal. Documentation placeholders are not accepted.

instanceUuid.description: Lowercase, identical to the pattern in database-port-allocations.schema.json. Two spellings of one identity are two identities to a string comparison, and the whole value of this field is that the two documents can be matched against each other.

jwkThumbprint.description: An RFC 7638 JWK thumbprint: the base64url SHA-256 of the canonical public key, so the identifier is a function of the key rather than a name somebody chose. 43 characters is the unpadded length; padding is not accepted, because a kid that compares unequal to itself across two encoders is a rotation that silently never completes.

providerId.description: A provider resource identifier or a non-secret client ID. Client secrets are excluded from this document entirely, not merely pattern-constrained.

timestamp.description: RFC 3339 UTC. Present only on the deployed branch: the rendered branch is byte-identical across renders and a timestamp would destroy that (plan decision U, extended by ADR 0012).

httpsUrl.description: No userinfo component, so a credential cannot be smuggled into a URL.

endpoint.description: Version 4 made the available case as constrained as the unavailable one. Through version 3 the conditional bound only `unavailable`, so a document could claim `available` with every field still null and validate -- an endpoint that says it exists and tells you nothing. Angle-bracket placeholders that resemble connection strings are not permitted, and the URL may not carry a password: `postgresql://role@host:port/db` is the shape, and a `role:secret@` userinfo fails the pattern rather than being redacted later by something that might forget.

postgresUrl.description: A role and a host, never a password. The userinfo component admits one identifier and no colon, so `postgresql://role:secret@host/db` cannot validate. This is the same rule `httpsUrl` states for the public surfaces, applied where it matters most.

lifecycle.description: Version 15 (ADR 0186). Carried from the manifest's `project.lifecycle`, or `permanent` when the manifest predates version 3 -- which is what every earlier manifest meant by saying nothing. Both branches carry it: the render says what the project is, and the deployed document repeats it so the fleet inventory can read it off the host without the manifest. `expires_at` is a fact an operator reads, never a trigger (D951).

accessProfiles.description: Version 4, ADR 0041. Three ways to reach two transports. The endpoints say *where*; these say *as whom*, so a reader can answer 'what may this credential do' without consulting the code. Each profile's transport is fixed by a const here rather than merely typed, because a profile named `runtime_pooled` that pointed at the direct transport would be a document that validates and lies.

accessProfile.description: `transport` and `role` are derivations and are present from the first render: the transport is fixed by the profile's name and the role comes from `naming`, so nulling them while unavailable would hide a fact the document already knows. `password_secret_ref` is the one member that waits, because a secret reference names something that must have been declared.

apiConnectionBudget.description: How many cluster connections the REST service commits to: its declared `api.rest.pool_size` plus the reservations `config.postgrest_connection_budget` adds. Published because the bootstrap plane reads only this document and cannot otherwise see a manifest figure, which is the half of D161's arithmetic that had nowhere to come from. The *application's* limit is deliberately absent: it is what the live server has left after this and the administration reserve, and a rendered document naming it would be publishing a guess about a server nobody has queried (D94). Version 8, ADR 0070.

storageSettings.description: Version 11 resolved the manifest's storage bounds into this block. The runtime reads them from HERE and never from the manifest, which is ADR 0002 applied to four numbers: this document is the one thing every plane reads, and a service re-reading the manifest would be a second authority for a bound the deploy was checked against. `bucket` and `prefix` were already this shape -- the manifest's values are overrides of a `naming` derivation, not inputs to one. There is no readiness claim here: whether the provider actually answers is `routes.storage`'s status on the deployed branch (D326), because a second convergence mechanism would need its own tests and its own failure modes beside one that is already proved on two projects. Shared by BOTH document kinds since D389: the deployed branch forbade this block entirely -- no property and additionalProperties false -- so a deployment published the storage ROUTE and none of the bounds that route enforces, and STO-BOUND-001 read the deployed document for max_upload_bytes and found nothing to measure. The sentence above says the runtime reads these from here, and the document the runtime actually reads is the deployed one. One definition rather than a copy per branch, because a copy is what let the two disagree.

prefix.description: The object key's first half, and `naming` is its single authority (ADR 0102). The second half -- `v1/<uuid4>` -- is generated per upload intent by `services/auth-api/app/object_keys.py`, which is the only place the two are ever concatenated. Nothing else spells `objects/`.

allowed_cors_origins.description: The ONE origin list for storage (D323). The edge middleware and the bucket's own CORS policy are two renderings of this array, tied together by a test -- two lists would be two policies that agree until one of them is edited.

backupSettings.description: The backup repository's identity and its one bound, version 13. ONE definition referenced from both branches, `storageSettings`' shape and for its measured reason (D389): a copy per branch is what let the two disagree, and STO-BOUND-001 read the deployed document for a bound that existed only on the rendered one. Every member here is derived or resolved by the deploy, so both branches carry the same values. `bucket` is a SEPARATE bucket from `storage.bucket` and that is ADR 0145 rather than a filing choice -- R2 scopes a token to buckets far more cleanly than to prefixes, so the isolation is a measured 403 rather than a policy sentence. `retain_full` is published whether or not backups are enabled, unlike the three identities beside it: it is a bound rather than a name, it was validated and read by NO code for nine sessions (D519), and nulling it would put 'the default is two chains' back where only source can answer it. What is NOT here is any observation -- see `backup_state`, which exists only on the deployed branch.

backupState.description: What was READ from the repository and the archiver, version 13, deployed branch only. `not_observed` with every other member null is the honest state for a deployment nothing has asked yet, and it is the value this block carries until Run 6 writes an observer -- the discipline `database.observed` and `endpoint` already use, for the reason they use it: a zero would be indistinguishable from a real measurement that happened to be zero. `unconfigured` is backups disabled, or enabled with no repository credential in the active generation, which is D326's two-stage convergence and not a failed deploy. `wal_failed_count` is here and `last_failed_wal` is not, because measurement (rig1, D535) showed the count is the value that MOVES while the segment name pins to the oldest stuck one -- a reader watching the name would see a steady value throughout the failure. `latest_recoverable_time` is a PROVEN FLOOR and never the clock (D529, D550): `pgbackrest info` has no latest-recoverable-time field at all -- measured in rig 6, it carries per-backup epochs and WAL SEGMENT NAMES, and a segment name has no time in or beside it -- so what is published is the newest backup's stop time, the latest instant this deployment can PROVE is recoverable. WAL archived afterwards extends real recovery past it, so a drill landing later is the floor being a floor rather than a contradiction, which is why the evidence document records the ACHIEVED recovery point as a field of its own. `awaiting_first_backup` is the state of every project between its first Session 10 deploy and its first operator-run full backup: the stanza exists and nothing can be restored yet. It is not `ready`, it is not a failure, and it is emphatically not `unconfigured` -- that value means a MISSING CREDENTIAL and would send an operator hunting for a secret that is present and correct (ADR 0149).
